nodes.name: Lebesgue's thesis on integral, length, and area
Numerical function language need not be tied to one analytic law, while remaining within nineteenth-century real-variable practice.
Discontinuous and highly irregular numerical assignments appear explicitly, but admissibility still depends on the integration framework.
Definite integrability is tested through convergence of subdivision sums and control of oscillation.
Riemann formulates a sum-based criterion for definite integration within the trigonometric-series investigation.
Functions discontinuous infinitely often in every interval become explicit test cases rather than automatic exclusions from integration.
Continuity is expressed through historically distinct variable-increment and infinitesimal frameworks rather than one shared modern epsilon-delta syntax.
Student notes from Weierstrass's teaching record an explicit bound on input variation corresponding to an arbitrarily small allowed function variation.
Heine's published function theory gives explicit small-error and small-increment conditions for continuity and uniform continuity.
Functions of roots are compared under permutations as part of solving and explaining algebraic equations.
Galois uses groups of permutations and substitutions within the solvability problem; this is not yet the later abstract group concept in its mature form.
Normal-section and analytic surface curvature before Gauss
Gauss's measure of curvature through the spherical image and metric formulas
Deformation-independent relations in Gauss's surface theory
Uniqueness is formulated by requiring every coefficient to vanish when a convergent trigonometric series has zero sum for every real argument, without assuming uniform convergence.
A finite number of exceptional arguments may be omitted from convergence or equality without destroying the uniqueness conclusion.
Certain infinite exceptional point sets are admitted when finite iteration of the derived-set operation eventually leaves only finitely many points.
For a linear point set P, P' is the set of limit points of P; finite iteration of this operation is used to distinguish point sets in the uniqueness theorem.
Kummer's ideal divisors were characterized through divisibility behavior in cyclotomic arithmetic, not as Dedekind's later systems of integers.
Dedekind's first ideal theory used systems of algebraic integers and still depended substantially on simple ideals represented by congruences.
Dedekind's later presentations increasingly foregrounded operations and properties of ideals rather than particular congruence representations.
Jordan assigns content to point sets in his 1892 treatment of definite integrals; later measure-zero boundary formulations are not part of this historical state.
Borel extends length from intervals to a wider family of point sets using countable set operations, without later abstract sigma-algebra terminology.
Borel's measurable-set construction uses countable set operations, and Lebesgue's 1901 note explicitly invokes Borel measurable sets in its measure-and-integration construction.
Lebesgue defines measure of point sets through countable open coverings in the 1901 note, before later outer-measure and completion terminology.
Lebesgue subdivides the range of function values, measures the corresponding sets of arguments, and forms sums from those measures to define the generalized integral.
Lebesgue's thesis develops measure of sets before integration and gives a fuller systematic development of the generalized integral introduced in 1901.
